title: Life-size replica of Chauvet Cave art in Vallon-Pont-d'Arc, France
caption: The past, unearthed
subtitle: International Archaeology Day
description:
Some discoveries start with a shovel. Others start with a drawing on a cave wall. International Archaeology Day celebrates both the detective work and the evidence behind them. Organised by the Archaeological Institute of America, this annual event began in 2011 and became International Archaeology Day in 2013 as participation expanded worldwide. Today, it brings archaeology closer to the public through talks, museum programmes, site visits, simulated digs and hands-on activities.
That detective mindset helped reveal the significance of Chauvet Cave in southern France. Discovered in 1994, the cave contains more than 1,000 drawings and engravings depicting at least 14 animal species, including mammoths, lions, rhinoceroses and bison. Dating back to roughly 35,000 years ago, the artwork offers evidence of early human creativity and artistic techniques. The original cave is carefully protected, so visitors can experience a detailed replica at Grotte Chauvet 2 in Vallon-Pont-d'Arc. Archaeologists combine excavation, documentation, scientific dating and modern imaging to turn such discoveries into clues about the past.

title: Dolbadarn Castle, Llanberis, Eryri National Park (Snowdonia), Wales
caption: 75 and thriving
subtitle: Eryri National Park (Snowdonia) in Wales turns 75
description:
If parks could keep birthday diaries, Eryri National Park (Snowdonia) in Wales would have quite the story to tell. The park turns 75 today, marking the anniversary of its designation in 1951. Eryri stretches across 2,130 square kilometres, with nine mountain ranges, 119 kilometres of coastline and habitats ranging from peatlands and native woodlands to upland landscapes. At more than 1,050 metres, Yr Wyddfa is Eryri's highest point. Nearby, the Carneddau and Glyderau add their own peaks, while Cadair Idris rises in the south. These protected landscapes provide habitats for wildlife and include 17 National Nature Reserves and 56 Sites of Special Scientific Interest.
And Eryri's story isn't just about nature. Dolbadarn Castle adds a medieval chapter. Built during the 13th century by Llywelyn the Great, the castle guarded the route through Llanberis Pass and later served as a prison for a Welsh prince. Its round tower, standing 15 metres tall, remains its most recognisable feature, overlooking nearby Llyn Padarn.

title: Grand Canal in Venice, Italy
caption: The road that runs on water
subtitle: Grand Canal in Venice, Italy
description:
What if a city's busiest street had no road? In Venice, Italy, traffic flows along the Grand Canal, a 3.8-kilometre waterway that winds through the city in a giant reverse S-shape. Known to locals as the Canalazzo, it is Venice's main water-traffic corridor, carrying vaporetti, water taxis, gondolas, police boats and other vessels. The canal follows the course of an ancient river that once flowed into the Venetian Lagoon.
Nearly 170 historic buildings line its banks, many built by wealthy Venetian families between the 13th and 18th centuries. With palaces and houses rising directly from the water, the Grand Canal has little room for conventional sidewalks.
Despite its importance, only four bridges cross it: Rialto, Scalzi, Constitution and Accademia. For centuries, boats were the main way to cross. Today, a journey along the canal offers a moving look at Venice's architecture and history. Here, even a traffic jam comes with a view—and a gondolier.

title: Brown-throated sloth, Puerto Viejo de Talamanca, Costa Rica
caption: Life in the slow lane
subtitle: International Sloth Day
description:
Slow and steady wins the race—and the brown-throated sloth seems perfectly happy to skip the race altogether. On International Sloth Day, this three-toed mammal offers a different lesson in getting by: conserve energy, hang on and take your time.
Native to Central and South America, it spends much of its life upside down in the forest canopy. Its coarse fur hosts algae, fungi and specialised sloth moths, creating a tiny ecosystem on its back. The algae can even give its coat a greenish tint, helping it blend into the foliage. Its unusual anatomy helps it thrive in the treetops. Its extra neck vertebrae allow it to turn its head up to 270 degrees.
Even digestion takes the slow lane. Its multi-chambered stomach helps break down tough, fibrous leaves. About once a week, it makes a risky trip to the forest floor to defecate. And despite its sluggish reputation, it is also a surprisingly capable swimmer.

title: Nguyen Hoang Bridge over the Perfume River, Hue, Vietnam
caption: Winging it over the river
subtitle: Nguyen Hoang Bridge, Hue, Vietnam
description:
Bridging the gap between old and new, Nguyen Hoang Bridge gives Hue's skyline a fresh connection. Spanning the Perfume River in Vietnam, the modern steel-arch landmark opened to traffic on March 26, 2025. Its design, called 'The Crane Facing Thien Mu,' draws inspiration from a local legend and nearby Thien Mu Pagoda.
Designed by Finnish bridge architect Antti Karjalainen, the bridge features steel arches shaped like a crane's outstretched wings. Its V-shaped piers suggest cranes gathering peacefully beside the river. The royal-yellow colour pays tribute to Hue's imperial heritage under the Nguyen dynasty.
The details continue along the pedestrian walkways, where 64 parasol-shaped steel ornaments echo the aesthetics of the royal court. After dark, colour-changing LEDs illuminate the arches, creating the appearance of a crane in flight. There is a historical twist, too: Hue's famous Truong Tien Bridge briefly carried the Nguyen Hoang name in 1945. With its mix of heritage and modern engineering, this bridge gives Hue a new way to move forward.

title: Fall in Naejangsan National Park, South Korea
caption: Still waters, vivid colours
subtitle: Fall in Naejangsan National Park, South Korea
description:
Few places in South Korea capture the magic of fall quite like Naejangsan National Park, where mountainsides glow in brilliant shades of scarlet, orange, yellow and gold. Located in the country's southwest, the park is particularly famous for its vivid maple colours, making it one of Korea's premier destinations for fall scenery. Its name, meaning 'many secrets in the mountains,' reflects the varied landscapes found throughout the region.
Naejangsan rises to more than 700 metres at Sinseonbong Peak, with nine distinctive peaks surrounding its valleys. Visitors can follow hiking trails through woodlands and mountain passes, while the Naejangsan Cable Car offers elevated views of the colourful ridgelines. The park is also home to the historic temples of Naejangsa and Baegyangsa, adding a rich cultural dimension to the landscape.
Other highlights include Geumseongyegok Valley and the Dodeokpokpo and Geumseonpokpo waterfalls. With around 760 species of native plants, Naejangsan offers rich biodiversity beyond its celebrated fall colours, making it a destination worth exploring in every season.

title: Two grey wolves Yellowstone National Park, Wyoming, United States
caption: Partners in the wild
subtitle: Wolf Awareness Week
description:
Two grey wolves move through the sagebrush of Yellowstone National Park in Wyoming, home to some of North America's most closely watched wolf packs. Their thick coats help them withstand harsh winters, and their keen senses make them skilled hunters and communicators.
During Wolf Awareness Week, people around the world recognise the important role that wolves play in healthy ecosystems. Grey wolves are highly social animals that typically live in family groups, or packs, and work together to hunt, defend their territory and raise their young. After disappearing from Yellowstone in the early 20th century, they were reintroduced to the park in 1995 as part of a landmark conservation effort that restored the species to one of its most iconic habitats.
Today, Yellowstone remains one of the best places to observe these predators, offering a glimpse into the lives of one of the continent's most celebrated wildlife species.

title: Royal Portuguese Cabinet of Reading, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil
caption: Bookishly extravagant
description: Today we're inside the Royal Portuguese Cabinet of Reading in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, where the humble act of opening a book took on grand architectural ambitions. Founded in 1837 by 43 Portuguese immigrants, just 15 years after Brazil's independence, the institution eventually moved into the building seen here, completed half a century later in a lavish Neo-Manueline style. Shelves soar over 20 metres around a vast reading room, crowned by a monumental stained-glass skylight that makes daylight part of the design.
